title: Logs platform
like: a label-indexed log service like Loki
brief: Build a shared log service for 2,000 teams. Collectors send compressed chunks, and on-call engineers find logs by tenant, service and time before filtering their words. A wide search or a runaway label must not stop other teams from investigating an outage.

clarify.q: Do we need arbitrary word search with no service or time filter?
clarify.a: It is allowed as a bounded asynchronous scan. Normal interactive queries specify tenant, service and a narrow time range. A label index is enough for this path; a full-text index is an optional paid tier.

clarify.q: What counts as an accepted chunk?
clarify.a: The API verifies a stable tenant-scoped chunk id and checksum, durably uploads the chunk, then acknowledges it. Search visibility may lag by up to a minute while index metadata is published. Collectors retain unacknowledged chunks and retry the same identity with backoff.
Keep ordinary compressed logs for 30 days and selected audit streams for a separate agreed retention policy. Redact secrets at collection. Never use request ids or user ids as stream labels.

The batch type represents a 100 MB compressed chunk, as in the catalog. Read represents a small chunk or index lookup, not an arbitrary full-text scan. Query fan-out, index cardinality and scanned bytes need separate sizing.

notes: At the flat planning rate, 1 chunk/s × 100 MB is about 8.64 TB/day and 259.2 TB over 30 days, before metadata and audit exceptions (approx.).
The score measures durable chunk acceptance and small reads. It does not model label index construction, text scan work, tenant fairness or redaction.

A catalog batch represents a 100 MB object upload, not one message sent through a standard queue. Object chunks are immutable. Stable chunk ids and sequence ranges make retries reconcilable; index publication follows durable upload.

The current sim applies a global request mix. All source paths share a real authenticated front door. workloadPlan records source-specific rates for a later engine; it is descriptive and does not affect this score.

numbers.label: One broad scan at 2 GB/s
numbers.how: 8.64 TB ÷ 2 GB/s, about 72 minutes for one full day, ignoring indexes and parallelism (approx.).

hints: Choose the index from the normal query shape. Which labels keep stream count bounded?
Keep immutable chunk uploads durable and separate from expensive query work. Limit scanned bytes and concurrency per tenant.

Use an authenticated front door and admission limits. Upload complete chunks directly to object storage, then publish label-index metadata. Cache immutable chunk reads with tenant-aware keys. Budget label-index memory and query fan-out separately.

editorial.summary: Authenticate tenants before admission. Collectors upload already compressed chunks through the API to object storage. Acknowledge only after durable object acceptance, then publish label and time metadata idempotently. Queries select chunks through that index before scanning text. The API fleet includes index publication, query coordination and reconciliation. The graph measures object uploads and small reads; it is a simplified label-indexed service, not a claim to reproduce Loki's ingest protocol.

designs.name: Durable chunks and bounded label queries
designs.why: Batch uploads go directly from the API to object storage; reads can use the cache. A 100 MB chunk is an object, not a standard queue message. The API publishes a derived label index only after the chunk is durable and exposes the indexing watermark. A reconciler finds uploaded chunks whose publication was interrupted. Chunk metadata must preserve enough information to rebuild the index.

tradeoffs: A label index avoids continuous full-text indexing cost, but broad word searches scan more chunk bytes. Bound them and show pending results.
Never publish an index pointer before its immutable chunk is durable. Orphan chunks can be reconciled later; dangling pointers create missing results. Retries reuse chunk ids and sequence ranges.

Immutable chunk bytes can be cached by tenant, object identity and authorization scope. Query-result keys also need labels, time bounds and query semantics. Late uploads change historical query results, so use a watermark with invalidation or a bounded TTL.
The rate limiter represents admission, not a proof of per-tenant fair queueing. Bound bytes/s, streams, new-stream rate, scan bytes and query concurrency, then use weighted queues or cells.
The catalog prices storage and small request operations. The worked scan example adds CPU, decompression and object-read amplification that the score cannot price accurately.
editorial.realWorld: At roughly 100 MB/s compressed, thirty days hold about 259 TB before metadata. At the catalog's $0.023/GB-month, that payload alone is about $5,962/month. Index size, temporary uploads, replication, query scans and people add cost (approx.).

correctness.prompt: A worker uploads a chunk, then crashes before publishing its label index entry. How do retries and readers avoid missing or duplicating logs?
correctness.discussion: Use a stable tenant-scoped chunk id and immutable content or a checksum that detects a conflicting retry. Persist publication state and reconcile uploaded chunks with committed metadata. Publish an index pointer only after object durability is confirmed. A repeated publication must be idempotent. Expose an ingestion watermark so a query can distinguish not-yet-indexed data from an empty result. The reference score does not verify this protocol, label cardinality, tenant authorization or redaction.

fields.label: Publication order
options: Publish the index when upload starts, then retry the object separately
Verify durable chunk, then publish pointer idempotently
fields.explanation: Readers must not observe a pointer to a missing chunk; orphan chunks can be reconciled.

fields.label: Tenant budget
options: Limit scanned bytes and concurrent queries per tenant
Give tenants equal HTTP request limits regardless of query width
fields.explanation: Wide scans consume far more work than small lookups; a global rate does not establish fairness.

correctness.limits: The traffic score does not validate index publication, scan amplification, tenant fairness or log contents.
